tagline.text: A small island in the Island Garden City of Samal, with coral and quiet white-sand beaches on the south side of Davao Gulf

location.label: Location
location.text: South of Samal City (IGaCoS), Davao Gulf, around Santa Cruz Port

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (day trip from Davao, per person)

children.text: Talikud Island sits in Davao Gulf as the second large island of Samal City. It is less developed than Samal's main island, so quiet white-sand beaches and coral areas remain. You can cross by boat from Davao's Santa Ana Wharf for a day trip or a simple overnight stay.

Talikud Island (also spelled Talicud locally) is one of the two large islands that make up the Island Garden City of Samal (IGaCoS) in Davao Gulf. The city consists of Samal Island, this island and several small islets around them, and it belongs to Davao del Norte province. On the map it lies just below the southwestern tip of Samal's main island, and from Davao City it looks like a long, low island across the gulf.

In a word, its appeal is "the less developed side of Samal." Large resorts line the northern and western coasts of Samal's main island, but Talikud has limited electricity and running water, and lodging is mostly cottages and tents. In return, the beaches have white sand mixed with broken coral and driftwood, the water is a clear turquoise, and protected coral and fish sanctuaries around Isla Reta put snorkeling spots close at hand. If you think of it as "an island where you take one boat from downtown Davao and relax for a day" rather than expecting fancy facilities, you will be happy with it.

There are two main ways to visit. The first is a day trip: take a regular boat from Davao's Santa Ana Wharf, spend the day at Isla Reta or at the beaches on the far side such as Babu Santa and Dayang, and return on an afternoon boat. The second is to stay a night in a resort cottage or tent and enjoy a barbecue and the stars. Divers sometimes visit the coral areas around Talikud by dive-center boat from Davao.

Note that this is not a heavily documented destination, and many blog posts and reviews are several years old. Boat fares, schedules and resort entrance fees change over the years, so treat the numbers here as a rough baseline and confirm directly at Santa Ana Wharf and with the resort before you go. This white-sand beach right next to the Santa Cruz pier is the most accessible beach, where the regular boats land. The water is clear and a coral and fish sanctuary is close by, so if you bring snorkeling gear you can get straight into the water.

A quiet beach on the far side of the island, reached from Isla Reta by motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) or a small boat. Past reviews say tent camping was popular here, and many describe it as a good place to relax for a day in a calm atmosphere.

blocks.title: Dayang Beach and the Old Pier Ruins

children.text: In front of the Dayang beach resort, the pillars of a collapsed old pier remain underwater and mark the boundary between two beaches. You can swim in the clear water and look around the pillars, and many travelers stayed a night in the cottages.
Protected coral areas and fish sanctuaries around the island can be enjoyed by anyone who can swim. Many places do not rent equipment, so bring your own mask, snorkel and life vest.

Davao dive centers run regular trips around Talikud. Names such as Angel's Cove, Mansud Wall and Linosutan Coral Gardens are known, and some centers offer introductory or fun dives. Ask the center about schedules and availability.

Most resorts rent out charcoal grills and allow you to bring your own food, and some offer a "paluto" service that cooks fish or seafood you bring, charged per kilogram. Buying seafood at the market and grilling it on the island is the island's signature way to enjoy a day.

blocks.title: Davao Gulf Views from the Boat

children.text: The boat ride itself is a highlight. As you leave Davao's skyline behind, the Samal coastline and resorts pass by, and on a clear day you can see high mountain ridges inland. The deck is low, so take care not to get your camera wet.

45 minutes to 1 hour 15 minutes
, and if departure is delayed you may wait at the wharf for more than an hour.
Arrive at Isla Reta or Santa Cruz pier and claim a cottage or shade near the beach. Entrance fees differ by resort.
Look around the edge of the sanctuary while snorkeling. On days with high waves, do not push it; just swim in shallow water.
Grill the seafood or meat you brought for lunch. Water and ice may be hard to buy on the island, so prepare them in Davao.
Check the return boat time again with a local. Afternoon boats stop early, so you should be at the pier before this time.
Return to Davao by boat. If you miss the last boat you will have to stay on the island overnight, so watch the clock.
Boat schedules change with weather and the number of passengers. It is best to confirm by text with the wharf or the resort the day before.

items.title: 2 Days, 1 Night
items.subtitle: A quiet night at Babu Santa and Dayang beaches

children.text: Cross from Davao on a morning boat and go from Isla Reta to Babu Santa or Dayang beach by habal-habal or small boat.
Swim and snorkel at the beach until check-in, and have lunch with the ingredients you brought.
Barbecue at the resort grill and watch the stars. Electricity is available only at certain hours in many places, so bring a flashlight and a power bank.
Take a walk on the morning beach, check out, and return to the pier in time for an afternoon boat.
Cottages are simple in ventilation and electricity. Do not expect air conditioning or hot showers.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO); check the airline timetable for times and fares.
From the airport you can reach the city by taxi or Grab, and a taxi is the easiest way from the city to Santa Ana Wharf.

items.title: Boat from Santa Ana Wharf, Davao

Seats cannot be reserved, and the wharf gets crowded on weekends.
You can also take a boat from Santa Ana Wharf to Kaputian at the southern end of Samal, then cross to Talikud by a small boat. One review says the Kaputian leg takes about
20 minutes
, but confirm the exact fare locally.
Dive-center boats also usually leave by this route or from Santa Ana Wharf.
From the pier to the beach resorts you can walk or take a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) or tricycle. Older reviews put a habal-habal at about
per person.
Depending on the resort, a private boat (bangka) may take you straight to the beach, and the fare varies with bargaining and the number of passengers.

Because you must cross by boat, a day with calm seas and good visibility matters. In general, departing on a dry-season morning is the most reliable, and since the wind can pick up in the afternoon on some days, leave some margin for the return boat.
Davao is known as a region relatively outside the Philippines' typhoon paths, but weather varies from year to year. Postpone your plans on days with a gale warning or suspended sea travel.

Lodging on Talikud centers on small resorts, cottages and tents at Isla Reta, Babu Santa and Dayang beaches. Reviews have listed fan cottages from about
(4 people), and tents in the

range. Some places have electricity only during part of the day, and some reviews say cottages have no outlets, so a power bank and flashlight are essential. Ask the resort directly for current prices and booking methods.

It is safest to prepare as if there are almost no restaurants or shops. The usual approach is to buy ingredients at a Davao city market and grill them on the resort's grill, and bring plenty of water, drinks, ice and snacks. Some resorts can get fish from local fishermen for you, but not always. You need cash, and an ATM is not something to count on.
Check the last return boat time again as soon as you arrive on the island. If you miss it, you must stay overnight.
Bring plenty of cash. It is safest to assume there is no ATM on the island.
Bring a snorkel mask, life vest, waterproof bag, hat and sunscreen. Many places have no equipment rental.
Wharves and beaches get crowded on weekends and boat seats cannot be reserved, so weekdays are much more relaxed.
Buy water, snacks, ice and drinks in Davao. Shops on the island are limited.
Take your plastic bags and trash back with you. On a small island, waste disposal is difficult.
Texting the resort in advance about booking, entrance fees, gear rental and cooking service can save you a wasted trip.
Do not step on or touch the coral, and use reef-friendly sunscreen.
Boat schedules and fares differ between reviews and are not certain, and sailings change with sea weather. Check the latest information at the wharf before you depart.
Many reviews are old, so fares, entrance fees and contact numbers may have changed.
Regular boats are often small bangkas rather than large vessels, so prepare for seasickness and getting wet when waves are high.
Medical facilities and mobile coverage on the island may be limited, so bring basic medicines.
Davao Gulf and Samal have seen security incidents in the past, so check your government's travel advisories and local news before departure.
Night-time return boats are dangerous, so move before sunset.

from Davao by boat, and worth combining if you have a longer itinerary.
The departure city, where Santa Ana Wharf is located. With the airport, hotels and markets, it is a good place to buy ingredients and water.
A small island that dive-center boats are known to visit together with Talikud. Ask the center about individual access.
An upscale resort area on the western coast of Samal's main island, sometimes visible in the distance from the boat. It caters mainly to hotel guests, so check separately whether visits are possible.
